summary:
Lunar South Pole Navigator is an interactive, browser-based mission-planning and science-communication tool built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. At the lunar South Pole, the Sun skims the horizon at low angles, meaning shifting a landing site by just a few kilometers can determine whether a lander enjoys near-continuous solar power or sits in permanent shadow.

Using real NASA LRO LOLA elevation models, ASU/LROC Lunaserv maps, and NASA JPL Horizons ephemerides, our web application lets users explore illustrative Artemis IV study sites or click any custom coordinates poleward of 85°S across any selected date window. Users can inspect a 360° Polar Horizon Sky-Plot showing local crater-wall obstructions, Sun paths, and Earth's libration figure-8, toggle between engineering (Planner) and plain-language (Explorer) modes, and compare up to four sites or launch dates side-by-side to evaluate mission resilience.
details:
Live Application: https://jvixaychack.github.io/lunar-landing-site-navigator/

Open-Source Repository: https://github.com/jvixaychack/lunar-landing-site-navigator

What It Does & How It Works Lunar South Pole Navigator transforms raw NASA planetary terrain and orbital ephemeris datasets into an accessible visual decision-support tool for mission planners, students, and the public:

  1. True South Pole Stereographic Mapping (IAU2000:30120): Built with OpenLayers 10 and proj4, the map streams live ASU/LROC Lunaserv WMS basemaps (LROC Wide Angle Camera imagery, LOLA shaded relief, and illumination layers) with an automatic offline fallback. Users can inspect five illustrative Artemis IV study locations (Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim 1, Connecting Ridge, Peak Near Shackleton), a Deep Crater Floor comparison point ~5 km away, or enter/click any custom coordinates poleward of 85°S to ray-trace a new horizon mask on the fly.
  2. 360° Polar Horizon Sky-Plot & 720-Hour Timeline Scrubber: Ray-traced 1°-resolution horizon profiles from NASA's LRO LOLA 80 m/pixel South Pole DEM (accounting for lunar spherical curvature and a 2.0 m observer mast height) are paired with hourly NASA JPL Horizons (DE441) Sun and Earth positions in the lunar Mean Earth (MEAN_ME) frame with zero atmospheric refraction. Users can scrub or animate (1x, 2x, 4x) through 30-day seasonal presets or pick custom UTC start dates to observe Earth's libration figure-8 wobble, solar clearance angles, longest continuous sunlight streaks, and Earth line-of-sight (LOS) communication windows.
    1. Planner Mode: Displays geometric sunlight availability, continuous streak durations, Earth LOS windows, and horizon zoom (-10° to +15°) for rapid engineering trade studies.
    2. Explorer (Educator) Mode: Translates complex orbital geometry into plain-language explanations of how local terrain and airless lunar conditions create extreme lighting contrasts compared to Earth.
    3. Multi-Scenario Comparison (2–4 Sites/Dates): Places up to four sites or launch windows side-by-side to evaluate schedule slips or alternate landing coordinates.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 7, Tailwind CSS v4, OpenLayers (ol), proj4, and Lucide React.
  • Scientific Data & Serverless Backend: Python 3.12 (numpy, pytest) for offline LOLA DEM ray-tracing and JPL Horizons data generation, plus a Node.js serverless proxy (api/ephemeris.js) with a deterministic Meeus/Cassini analytical ephemeris fallback for offline static hosting on GitHub Pages.

Super Intelligence (SI) / AI Disclosure Super Intelligence (SI) tools—specifically Google Antigravity (Gemini 4 Hydrogen) and Claude Sonnet 5.5—were used to accelerate software scaffolding, UI restyling, TypeScript/React component implementation, Python ephemeris pipeline generation, and documentation drafting. All scientific formulas, NASA dataset integrations, coordinate transformations, and UI verifications were reviewed, tested, and validated by the team.
